u0: Name the Feeling You Are Avoiding
u2: Most putting-off is not laziness. It is avoiding an uncomfortable feeling. Name it, and it loses its power.
u3: Notice the moment you turn away from the task toward your phone, TV or a chat
u4: Ask: "What feeling am I trying to escape: boredom, confusion, fear of failing, feeling stupid, overwhelm?"
u5: Name it out loud: "I feel confused, and I don't like it"
u6: Breathe out slowly and say: "I can feel this and still start"
u7: Do the smallest first step for two minutes
u9: "Lazy" is usually a cover word; look underneath for boredom, fear or tiredness
u11: Use a feelings list, or notice where your body tightens
u13: It may be anxiety or low mood; talk to someone you trust
u14: Research suggests procrastination is mainly a way to regulate emotions: the brain's threat and discomfort systems push us toward quick relief. Naming the feeling calms the amygdala and lets the prefrontal cortex choose the task again.
u15: When you don't want to start something, ask: "What feeling am I running away from?" Say it, breathe, and start a tiny bit.
u16: Shrink It Until It Feels Easy
u18: If a task feels heavy, make the first step so small that your brain stops resisting.
u19: Write the task you keep avoiding
u20: Ask: "What is the smallest possible first step?" (open the book, tune the guitar, read one verse)
u21: Make it smaller again if you still feel resistance
u22: Do only that step, and stop if you want to
u23: Notice that starting is usually the hardest part, then decide whether to continue
u24: It feels too small to matter
u25: Small starts build the habit of starting; size comes later
u26: I always stop after the tiny step
u27: That is fine at first; grow it slowly each week
u28: I don't know what the first step is
u29: Ask a teacher or friend to break it down with you
u30: The brain estimates the effort cost of a task before starting. Shrinking the first step lowers that cost, so the reward system lets you begin, and momentum makes continuing easier.
u31: If a job feels too big, do a tiny piece of it, like opening your book. Tiny starts are easy, and then you keep going.
u32: Pair It With Something You Enjoy
u34: Link a task you avoid with something you love, so your brain starts to look forward to it.
u35: Choose one task you avoid: practice, revision, Bible reading, exercise
u36: Choose a small pleasure: a favourite drink, a cosy corner, worship music, a walk
u37: Allow the pleasure only while doing the task
u38: Keep the pairing for two weeks
u39: Notice whether the task starts to feel lighter
u41: Choose a pleasure that doesn't compete for attention, like tea or a pleasant place
u42: I cheat and take the pleasure anyway
u43: Make the pairing visible, or ask a friend to join you
u45: Even adults learn by reward; God gives good gifts
u46: Pairing a dull task with a reward teaches the dopamine system to anticipate pleasure, so the task itself begins to feel rewarding over time (temptation bundling).
u47: Do a boring job together with something you like, such as your favourite drink. Soon the boring job feels nicer.
u48: Design Your Space for the Good Habit
u50: Make the good thing easy and the distracting thing hard. Your environment decides more than your willpower.
u51: Choose the habit you want: practice, study, prayer
u52: Make it obvious: leave the guitar on its stand, the Bible open on the chair, the books on the desk
u53: Make distractions hard: phone in another room, log out of apps, TV remote in a drawer
u54: Set a fixed place and time for the habit
u55: Check after a week what helped and what didn't
u57: Use a corner, a bag or a box that means "this is my study or prayer space"
u59: Use focus mode, grayscale and app limits during that time
u61: Ask someone to keep it for you for the session
u62: Cues in the environment trigger habits automatically. Adding friction to distractions and removing friction from good habits changes behaviour without relying on willpower, which tires quickly.
u63: Put good things where you can see them and phones far away. Then doing the right thing is easier.

u98: Every excuse hides a real barrier. Find it and plan around it.
u99: Write the excuse exactly as you say it: "I didn't have time", "I'll do it later", "I wasn't in the mood"

u160: Find a Partner, Not a Pusher

u174: People are wired for connection, and working alongside others (sometimes called body doubling) helps attention and motivation. Encouragement activates reward circuits; nagging activates threat and resistance.
